candidates.title: An auto-push hook bound to file-edit events does not cover commits made through the shell
candidates.body:
CopyPasteLabs auto-commits and pushes via a PostToolUse hook whose matcher is `Write|Edit`. A commit created with `git commit` from the shell is not a Write or an Edit, so the hook never fires and nothing pushes. The result is that the *incidental* path (a stray file edit) is protected and the *deliberate* path (the well-messaged end-of-session commit the charter asks for) is not - the exact inversion of what you want. The failure is silent: the working tree is clean, the commit exists, the log looks healthy, and only `git status -sb` reveals `ahead 1`. In a single-writer repo where the remote is the only channel to other people, that silence is the whole cost.

Generalizes to any hook-based safety net: enumerate the paths that reach the protected state, not the tool calls you expect to be used. A net defined by tool name will be defined wrongly.
candidates.basis: Commit b3db63b (Lab v0 Milestone 2 component 3, 10 files) was made on 2026-08-19 and was still unpushed when this session started on 2026-08-21; `git status -sb` reported `ahead 1` and origin/master stood at 98a7b7a. `.claude/settings.json` shows the PostToolUse matcher is `Write|Edit` and scripts/autosave.sh is the only thing that pushes.

candidates.title: End-Session's upstream_merge_base boundary degenerates to base==head in a repo that auto-pushes
candidates.body:
Phase 2 resolves the session boundary by the first strategy that yields a commit. Strategy 1 (previous_inbox_entry) cannot fire on a first run. Strategy 2 (session_start_marker) never fires - prompt section D.2 already records that the marker holds a timestamp, not a SHA. That leaves strategy 3, `git merge-base HEAD origin/<branch>`, which returns HEAD itself whenever the branch has been pushed. CopyPasteLabs pushes after every file edit by design, so strategy 3 will essentially always return HEAD.

Consequence: `commits: []` and `changes.files: []` for a session that demonstrably made a commit. The evidence file - the half of the entry that is supposed to be the verifiable one - is empty, and Phase 3 attribution has nothing to attribute, so the entry falls back to `_platform` regardless of which project was worked on.

Strategy 1 will cover subsequent runs, so this is worst on a first run and after any gap. Three candidate fixes, none obviously right: capture before pushing (fragile, and fights autosave); make session-start.sh write the HEAD SHA alongside the timestamp so strategy 2 becomes real (cheap, and section D.2 already anticipates it); or reorder so a marker-derived base outranks merge-base. Recorded as a question, not a decision - this is Knowledge-Promoter's and the operator's call.
candidates.basis: This run. `git merge-base HEAD origin/master` returned 0e95642, identical to HEAD, because the reconciliation commit had been pushed minutes earlier. Phase 4 therefore recorded zero commits and zero changed files for a session that produced commit 0e95642 (6 files, +242/-24).

candidates.title: Write through shell heredocs to keep a PostToolUse hook from racing a multi-file operation
candidates.body:
End-Session prompt section D.1 documents an unsolved race: the PostToolUse `Write|Edit` hook fires after every file write, so a skill that writes seven files gets seven `Auto-save:` commits interleaved into the middle of its own run, and Phase 9 finds nothing left to commit. The prompt states the proper fix is outside its reach because it needs a `.claude/settings.json` change.

There is a cheaper move: write the files with shell heredocs instead of the Write/Edit tools. The hook matches on tool name, so a heredoc write does not trip it. The whole operation stays uncommitted until it chooses to commit, and one intentional commit with a real message is possible.

**State the caveat plainly: this is a workaround that defeats a safety net, not a fix.** It works because the matcher is narrow - the same narrowness recorded as a defect in cand-001. Anything written this way is unprotected until the explicit commit, so it is only safe when the operation ends in a commit it controls. Suppressing the hook explicitly for the duration of a run remains the honest fix.
candidates.basis: This session wrote the 2026-08-19 session log and patched five documents entirely through Bash heredocs and a Python script. No `Auto-save:` commits appeared, the tree stayed dirty until chosen, and the whole reconciliation landed as one commit (0e95642) with an explanatory message. The section D.1 race did not occur.

candidates.title: A blocker that has silently been cleared is as damaging as a stale fact, and harder to see
candidates.body:
Documentation review looks for facts that have gone out of date. It does not usually look for *constraints* that have gone out of date, and those are worse: a stale fact misleads a reader, but a false blocker stops work that could proceed, and it does so with the full authority of a recorded decision. Nobody argues with a checkbox.

The tell is a contradiction between a document and the environment it describes - here, a checkbox saying an API key must not be requested, sitting beside a populated API key. That contradiction is mechanically detectable in a way a stale prose claim is not, which suggests blockers deserve a cheap periodic check against reality rather than trust.

The repair matters as much as the detection. Recording the clearance without its provenance would substitute one false record for another, so both documents now say the clearance was recorded from memory rather than a contemporaneous note, and that any specific term must be re-read and quoted rather than recalled.
candidates.basis: `lab/v0-ingestion/README.md:134` and `roadmap.md:52` both carried an unchecked box reading "Do not request or fill this in until Milestone 0's blocker is cleared", while `.env.local` already held a 36-character SARVAM_API_KEY and `.env.example` carried the same instruction. The operator confirmed the terms had in fact been read and the vendor choice stands. The 2026-08-11 audit had already found the same class of error in this project - a README justifying Lab v0 with a mandate the frozen walkthrough protocol does not contain.

candidates.title: This Inbox has no consumer: Knowledge-Promoter is a stub, so nothing can leave staging
candidates.body:
CLAUDE.md v2.0 routes every candidate through `AI-Memory/Inbox/` and names Knowledge-Promoter as the sole writer of permanent memory and INDEX.md. Six manual commands ("Promote this", "Demote this", "Refactor memory", and the promotion half of the others) terminate in that skill. It does not exist: `specification.md` is v0.0.0 marked Placeholder and holds only the interface contract End-Session was built against; `prompt.md` says "Status: NOT WRITTEN".

So capture now works and curation does not. The charter's own stated failure mode - "if the Promoter is never run, the Inbox becomes a landfill" - is currently guaranteed rather than risked, because there is nothing to run. This entry is the first item in that backlog.

The open question is scope, and it is genuinely open: the Promoter's own specification lists duplicate merging as "this skill's core work and its hardest part" and does not settle where the human sits in the loop. A deliberately minimal first version - read pending entries, promote or reject with a human deciding each, defer merging - may be worth more than a complete one, but that is a decision to take, not an assumption to act on.
candidates.basis: `AI-Memory/Inbox/` did not exist on disk before Phase 1 of this run created it. No commit in the repository's history carries the `Session capture:` prefix. Permanent AI-Memory holds four substantive entries, all dated 2026-07-28, while project work ran through 2026-08-19. `Skills/Knowledge-Promoter/prompt.md` reads "Status: NOT WRITTEN".

candidates.title: Write the failure condition into the decision that might fail, and drift becomes detectable
candidates.body:
A decision that records only its reasoning can only be re-argued. A decision that also records the observable event that would mean it went wrong can be *checked* - and the check costs one line of reading, needs no judgement, and does not reopen the original argument.

The condition has to be an event someone will actually observe, not a metric someone must remember to measure. "If the next session again ends with X and no Y" is checkable by anyone reading the next session's log. "If velocity drops" is not.

The value showed up in an unexpected place. The condition was written by the people making the decision, so when it fired there was no argument about whether it counted - the decision had already conceded the point in advance. That converts a judgement call, which a session under time pressure will duck, into a lookup. The cost is real: it requires naming, at the moment of greatest optimism about a choice, the specific way you expect it to go wrong.
candidates.basis: `Projects/classmind/.knowledge/decisions.md:89-92` (2026-08-11) reads: "The failure mode to watch: Lab v0 becoming the reason the walkthrough keeps slipping. If the next session again ends with Lab progress and no walkthrough date, that is this decision going wrong, and the answer is to stop building and book the day." The next session, 2026-08-19, ended with Lab progress and no walkthrough date. The condition was recognised as met at the start of this session by reading two documents, with no re-litigation of the original decision.

candidates.title: When an SDK error carries both status and statusCode, check both and normalize the type
candidates.body:
A not-found probe tested `error.status === 404`. The Supabase Storage SDK reports a missing bucket as `status: 400` with `statusCode: "404"` - the meaningful code is in the other field, as a string. Strict equality against a number therefore returned false, the probe read "not found" as a fatal error, and the resource could never be created. The provisioning script could not succeed on a fresh project, which is the only situation it exists for.

Two things generalize. An error object exposing two similarly named code fields is a signal that they carry different things - usually a transport-level status and a service-level one - so check both rather than picking the better-named one. And `===` against an SDK-supplied code assumes a type the SDK never promised; coerce, then compare.

The wider point is about which bugs the happy path hides: this one is invisible when the resource already exists and fatal exactly once, on first run, in a code path nobody re-tests.
candidates.basis: `Projects/classmind/lab/v0-ingestion/scripts/setup-storage.mts` - `isNotFound()` tested `error.status === 404`; the SDK returned `status` 400 with `statusCode` "404" as a string, so the bucket-existence probe was misread as fatal and the bucket could never be created. Found and fixed on 2026-08-19 while provisioning the backend; normalized to a number.
